summary:
İzmir stands under the national framework of Turkey. No İzmir-specific signal on trans legal status, policing or facilities was identified in the source inventory; the national assessment applies, and İzmir's own exposure should be read through the documented national pattern of street identity checks. On 31 July 2025 police in a large-city entertainment district conducted mass identity-document roundups of trans women, recording names and filming them without giving any official reason, a practice bianet links to profiling concerns.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would amend civil code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing deemed-illegal interventions would face fines and up to seven years' prison, and trans people receiving such care up to three years, with courts able to order pretrial detention. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment into unregulated underground settings. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. It records 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025, roughly two and a half times the previous year, citing detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants as the main reasons; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations; and six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected. For the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy.
tangentialFactors: The draft package's civil-code amendment would raise the age for gender-affirming care to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility, a provision that would reshape what care a trans resident or long-term visitor could lawfully obtain and under what conditions. The Kaos GL figures are national counts for 2025 and are reported as raw totals without a per-capita denominator, so they indicate scale of state action rather than a comparative risk ranking between Turkish cities.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of İzmir live under the same national custody regime documented elsewhere in Turkey: detention facilities are organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and LGBTI+ detainees are subject to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare, with no policy or staff training to identify LGBTI+ needs. Complaints procedures are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so residents must obtain and pay for it privately.

The closure of an LGBTI+ association and criminal cases against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy, recorded in the Kaos GL 2025 report, signal reduced space for organised advocacy that İzmir's own LGBTI+ groups would face.
outOfScopeNotes: Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since Human Rights Watch's 29 October 2025 report is unresolved in the sources. The inventory contains no İzmir-specific incidents, policing practice or local ordinance; the identity-check account of 31 July 2025 is described only as occurring in a large-city entertainment district and is not attributed to İzmir. No source in this inventory documents İzmir-specific violence, facility access or official statements.
